Memorandum
To: Interested Parties
From: Brian Galle (UC Berkeley), David Gamage (University of Missouri), and Darien
Shanske (UC Davis)1
Re: Analysis of the Impacts of Propositions 41 and 42 on California’s Public Finance
Date: August 20, 2026
Introduction
In this memorandum, we will discuss the potential impacts of Propositions 41 and
42 on current and future initiatives and legislation, as well as on current California
Medicaid tax programs, starting with possible impacts on Proposition 3, the measure on
November’s ballot to extend personal income tax rate increases.
The purpose of the memo is to identify legal risks raised by the propositions that
prudent citizens should be aware of given the high stakes. We are not arguing how a court
should decide these issues and we do not claim that we are offering the best or most
persuasive legal arguments. We do, however, believe that there is a real risk courts could
reach these outcomes.
Our bottom line is that both propositions are poorly drafted in a manner that could
pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key
spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises. That is not
surprising. These are deceptive measures that were drafted quickly to trick voters that
support the billionaire wealth tax (Prop 40) into voting for competing measures that could
undermine that tax. The billionaire funders of these initiatives are acting with reckless
disregard for the collateral damage to California’s fiscal system and indeed they may even
benefit from weakening California’s existing taxes affecting the most wealthy.
Executive Summary
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could hamstring Proposition 3 (the
teacher-sponsored measure to fund education with taxes on million-dollar earners)
or invalidate it outright.
1 Institutional affiliations are listed for identification purposes only.
2
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could similarly hamstring many other
revenue raising measures, such as (for example) a tax on large employers who have
many employees on Medi-Cal.
• The prohibition on easing the state appropriation limit in Proposition 41 could
undermine many existing and proposed taxes to fund California’s contributions to
Medi-Cal, including current MCO taxes and the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee
(HQAF).
• The limitations on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could impact the
ability of the state to tax capital gains income, whether as part of Proposition 3 or
otherwise.
• The limitation on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could frustrate any
future attempt to reform California’s Vehicle License Fee, a backbone tool for
financing a wide array of local services.
Proposition 41
Proposition 41 makes two significant changes to California law. First, it adds many
new audit requirements, specifically pre-election audits of programs that would receive
funds from a proposed special tax initiative; and recurring audits, every four years, of
programs receiving moneys from special taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026,
whether enacted by the Legislature or by initiative.2 Second, the proposition prohibits
collecting any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026 that is exempted
or excluded from the appropriations limit of Article XIIIB, the so-called Gann limit, whether
the exemption comes from an outside-the-General-Fund special fund whose spending is
not counted or from raising the limit itself. Proposition 41, secs. 3, 4(b). The obvious point
of this second change, hidden deep in the Proposition 41 text, is to nullify Proposition 40.
But both changes would likely weaken California public finance by threatening California’s
ability to raise revenues and fund spending programs.
On the Merits
Prop 41 targets the primary (and, in many cases, the only plausible remaining) way
that state tax policy can be done and that state services can be adequately funded. Any
increase in taxes enacted by the Legislature requires a two-thirds supermajority of each
house.3 Statewide initiatives, by contrast, can raise taxes by majority vote. Not surprisingly,
most major tax policy changes over recent decades have therefore occurred via initiative.
Since voters are unlikely to support tax increases for unspecified purposes, the limits on
2 Prop. 41, Secs. 1, 2.
3 Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
3
measures adopting taxes for specified purposes tilts the deck against most of those
measures. Even if there were eventually an attempt to change Prop 41 through another
ballot measure, the pre-election audit requirement would still apply to any special tax
initiatives on that ballot.
The audits that Prop 41 would impose are slanted to make it more difficult to adopt
and fund new programs. Consider, for example, that a pre-election audit must consider:
“How the program's costs compare to any analogous programs in the non-government
sector”; and also: “Recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary
savings of at least 10% annually.” The audits would thus institutionalize a cost-cutting,
private-sector-comparison framework, and the executive summary of the pre-election
audit would be printed in the voter guide immediately after the Legislative Analyst’s
impartial analysis.4
In sum, every proposed special tax initiative would come before the voters bundled
with an official analysis oriented toward finding savings and private alternatives. These
expensive, burdensome and largely redundant5 requirements would hinder special tax
initiatives, making them more difficult to pass and less effective if passed.
The second provision regarding the Gann limit would double down on what has
proven to be a disastrous set of fiscal policies. The existing Gann limit works by capping
government expenditures over a given two-year period. Excess amounts must be split
between taxpayer rebates and education.6 The cap increases only to the extent of growth in
California population and cost of living.7 Given the increasing demands on the state
government, future uncertainties, and the changing nature of federal assistance, the limit
does not act so much as a ceiling as a vise squeezing out funds for core services.8 For
example, what happens if the state government needs to spend more on (say) wildfires? Or,
4 Sec. 1(e)(2).
5 California law is already full of audit requirements and indeed has a powerful and independent
state auditor (Govt Code 8543 et seq, see especially GC 8546.1) that issues regular,
https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/, and, often critical, reports about state operations. See, e.g.,
https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/reponses-2025-108-all/. And sometimes the state requires
particular audits. See, e.g., Bus. And Prof. Code 6145(b). As further discussed, the income tax
extensions authorized by Proposition 3 are already subject to audit. Art. XIII, Sec. 36(g).
6 Art. XIIIB, Sec. 2.
7 Art. XIIIB, Secs. 8(e), (f).
8 Making a similar point, here is Jason Sisney (an Assembly budget insider): “Therefore, if revenues
push the state to its Gann limit, non-Proposition 98 programmatic spending (such as annual tax-
supported spending on health and human services (HHS), housing, universities, prisons, state
employees and natural resources programs) probably would have to be cut more in this situation.”
https://jasonsisney.substack.com/p/state-moving-closer-to-its-appropriation
4
what if the state government must spend more to backfill vicious cuts from the federal
government?
The state has hit the Gann limit recently (2022) and is about $30 billion under the
Gann limit currently. Suppose Prop 3 passes without incident and the AI boom does lead to
substantial increases in revenue. At that point, the state will be close to the limit. Any
possible new initiatives for education, child care, housing or wildfire abatement could then
well go over the limit.
Threats to Proposition 3
The audit requirements of Proposition 41 arguably apply to Proposition 3 because
Proposition 3 would seem to impose a “special tax” enacted “by a statewide initiative
measure on or after January 1, 2026.” Sec. 2(a)(1). Proposition 3 makes permanent the
existing 1% tax surcharge on income above $1 million that is set to expire in 2030; all of its
revenues are earmarked primarily for education. It thus likely involves a “special tax,”
which is “a tax that can only be used to fund specific, as opposed to unlimited, purposes”
(according to Prop 41), because the Education Protection Account revenues added by Prop
3 may be used only for specified education and health care purposes. Sec. 4(d) of
Proposition 41; Article XIII, Sec. 36(e) of Proposition 3.
As for whether Proposition 3 was enacted after January 1, 2026, a court could
plausibly find that a tax first approved in 2012 is “enacted” in 2026 when the voters delete
its sunset. The new provision is different than the old in that it will never expire; the post-
2030 tax will exist only because of the 2026 vote; and the adoption of the extension is itself
literally an enactment.9
Thus, Proposition 41 might plausibly be interpreted by courts as applying to
Proposition 3. If so, Proposition 41 would require onerous and burdensome audits of the
programs it funds.
Further, if both measures pass and Proposition 41 receives more affirmative votes,
every provision of Proposition 3, including the rate extension itself, could be ruled void.
The terms of Proposition 41 state that it nullifies other conflicting 2026 initiatives if it
receives more votes. Prop 41 defines conflicting measures as “another initiative measure
9 Notably, neither Prop 41’s prohibition nor its grandfather clause discusses extensions, even
though California drafters know how to address extensions expressly. For instance, Proposition 218
reaches taxes that governments “impose, extend, or increase,” and the Proposition 218
implementation statute treats removal of a sunset as an extension. Art. XIII C, Sec. 2(b); Gov. Code
Sec. 53750(e).
5
that …imposes different audit rules on special taxes.” Sec. 5(a). Proposition 3 carries
forward Proposition 30’s audit rules, and those rules are different from Proposition 41’s.10
Threats to the MCO Tax
The sloppy drafting of Proposition 41 implicates policies far beyond Proposition 3.
We will briefly consider spending on health care.
Start with the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax, which California expects to
generate as much as $8 billion annually in federal matching funds. There are now arguably
two separate MCO provisions that will take effect after 2026 authorization, both of them
threatened by Prop 41.
The first is SB 125, enacted in June 2026, which imposes a tax of $8.85 per enrollee
per month for 2027 through 2029 and deposits the proceeds in the new Medi-Cal Stability
Fund, dedicated to specified Medi-Cal purposes.11 SB 125 is a special tax enacted after
January 1, 2026, so under Prop 41 each Medi-Cal program receiving its moneys would face
recurring State Auditor financial and performance audits, with the private-sector
comparisons and ten percent savings recommendations, and with the Auditor reimbursed
from the tax revenues themselves.12 As explained above, this would be very burdensome
and problematic. And because the Stability Fund broadly co-funds managed care payments
and rates, there is a further risk that a court would rule that the auditable “programs”
include major portions of Medi-Cal managed care, rather than just the marginal SB 125
dollars. Thus Prop 41 could require the state to pay for audits recommending how to
privatize Medi-Cal and slash it by 10%.
Proposition 41 also deprives the state of flexibility to keep SB 125 effective in the
future. As enacted, the SB 125 tax uses up capacity under the Gann limit, narrowing room
for other revenue needs. SB 125 also sunsets in 2030, at a time when there might not be
room under the Gann limit available for renewal. In both cases, the state could be left
choosing between crowding out other priorities under the limit or losing the tax—and the
10 Indeed, on one point the two measures give seemingly incompatible commands about the same
dollars. Proposition 41 provides that the State Auditor “shall be reimbursed from the revenue
generated by the special tax” for the reasonable costs of its audits. Sec. 2(d). Section 36 (Proposition
3), however, provides that moneys deposited in the Education Protection Account for education
“shall not be used to pay any costs incurred by the Legislature, the Governor, or any agency of state
government,” and it separately bars using Account funds for administrative costs. Art. XIII, Sec.
36(e)(5), (6).
11 Ch. 24, Stats. 2026 (SB 125), adding a new Article 7.2 to the Welfare and Institutions Code; the
new tax is expressly made not subject to Proposition 35's chapter. See Dept. of Finance, Manual of
State Funds, Fund 3492 (Medi-Cal Stability Fund classified as included).
12 Sec. 2.
6
federal matching grants it secures— altogether. This would of course have major negative
implications for state funding of Medi-Cal.
In addition, in 2024, Proposition 35 implemented a permanent MCO tax starting in
2027.13 Proposition 35 also used a provision of the Gann limit, Art. XIIIB, Sec. 4, to lift the
ceiling for four years in order to accommodate the new spending.14 Recall that Prop 41
prohibits collecting any tax that modifies the Gann limit if the tax takes effect on or after
January 1, 2026. 15 There is thus a significant risk Prop 41 would prevent Proposition 35
from taking effect.
Threats to the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee (HQAF)
Prop 41 could also bar modifications to the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee (HQAF),
including modifications that might be required by the federal government in order for the
HQAF to remain in effect. The HQAF draws down billions of dollars in federal matching
funds for hospital payments, and the federal government approved the 2025 program in
June 2026. HQAF funds are exempt from the Gann limit.16 A court might conclude that an
HQAF modified after January 1, 2026 “takes effect” after that date for purposes of Prop 41.
That would prevent California from modifying or improving the HQAF, even if required by
federal rule changes, such as those now pending. A Trump or other hostile HHS aware of
this dilemma might go out of its way to require HQAF changes that it knows California
cannot implement.17
We expect that California would argue the HQAF is not subject to Prop 41 limits
because it is a “fee,” not a “tax,” but a court might well rule otherwise. This is because
Proposition 41 does not define “state tax” and because California generally interprets
“taxes” quite broadly. See Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(b). A multibillion dollar charge that funds not
only services for the payors but also transfers to others, as the HQAF does, will be quite
likely to face a plausible challenge that it constitutes a tax and not a fee.
Note that the stakes of these threats are further magnified because the statute
makes it so that the hospital fee becomes inoperative if a lawsuit is filed and a preliminary
13 Welf. & Inst. Code § 14199.123(b).
14 Proposition 35, Sec. 2.
15 Prop. 41, Secs. 3, 4(b)(2).
16 Cal. Const., art. XVI, § 3.5(d); Dept. of Finance, Manual of State Funds (Hospital Quality Assurance
Revenue Fund classified as excluded from the state appropriations limit). The Finance fund record
predates Proposition 52 and is based on the notion that the revenues are not proceeds of taxes;
Proposition 52 is the source of the constitutional exclusion.
17 It could also be argued that the HQAF takes effect after Jan. 1, 2026 even if it is not modified after
that date. This is because its mechanics operate through discrete, numbered program periods, and
each of these has its own fee model and its own federal approval. Thus, a period beginning after
January 1, 2026 could well be characterized as the tax taking effect after that date.
7
injunction or other order results in a loss of federal financial participation or any net
General Fund cost.18 A qualifying preliminary injunction or other order could thus obstruct
the program well before any final judgment, even if the challenge might ultimately fail on
the merits.
Threats to the Skilled Nursing Facility Fees
Yet another health funding source at risk from Proposition 41 is the skilled nursing
facility quality assurance fee (SNF-QAF). Like the HQAF, this is a provision intended to
generate federal matching funds, and it is expected to bring in several billion dollars over
the next 5 years. The SNF-QAF was extended by the Legislature in July 2026 through the
end of 2027,19 and its revenues are also classified as exempt from the Gann limit. Thus, a
court could well decide based on these arguments that collection of the fee should be
barred, thereby cutting off the federal matching funds and supplemental payments to
nursing facilities that the program exists to generate.
Single-Subject Threats
It is also possible that Prop 41 could make it impossible for any future initiative to
be exempt from the Gann limit, yoking California to the fiscal system of the distant 1970s in
perpetuity. The California Constitution requires that an initiative “embracing more than
one subject” may not be submitted to the voters or have any effect.20 Because Proposition
41's restrictions would be added to the Constitution (if they pass), a future revenue
measure could escape the restrictions only by pairing its new tax with a constitutional
override of Proposition 41. This thus gives opponents of any future revenue measure a
powerful new tool for challenging such measures through litigation. That is, future
initiatives would have to have what are arguably two subjects: their own goals, and also
disabling the Prop 41 rules.
It might be objected in regard to this that provisions suspending Prop 41 rules that
would frustrate a future initiative are part of a single subject, much as today many
initiatives suspend the Gann limit . But would such a structure be effective? The initiative
would now both impose a tax and change the separate constitutional rule that Prop 41
added as to the Gann limit. Arguably, a court could find that these are two separate subjects
that would require two separate measures. Although California’s single-subject test is
lenient, and a combined measure could thus potentially survive challenge, even just the
18 Welf. & Inst. Code § 14169.72.
19 SB 165, signed July 6, 2026; see Dept. of Finance, Manual of State Funds, Fund 3213 (Long-Term
Care Quality Assurance Fund classified as excluded).
20 Art. II, Sec. 8(d).
8
prospects of litigation and the increased potential for challenges could add uncertainty,
substantial and burdensome costs, and delays to any future revenue measures.
Relatedly, this same single-subject concern suggests (to us) that Proposition 41 (and
also 42) might be constitutionally infirm themselves as violating the single-subject rule. We
might suggest that a court should strike them down if they should pass.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 does at least three things: 1) it offers unneeded21 protection of
retirement assets; 2) it prohibits a tax “on the ownership or control of . . . individually-
owned assets” and 3) it prohibits retroactive taxes. As with Proposition 41, though, Prop
42’s deceptive framing and sloppy language has the potential to cause great collateral
harm.
Threats to Proposition 3
Because of Proposition 42’s broad language, taxpayers will likely argue that it
shields them from the effects of Prop 3. Again, Prop 3 extends the existing but temporary
1% additional income tax on incomes above $1 million, which is set to expire in 2030. Like
Proposition 41, Proposition 42 exempts taxes “in effect, imposed, and first collected” before
2026, and it is uncertain whether a court would find that Proposition 3 qualifies for that
exemption. A court might deem the permanent post-2030 additional income tax on
incomes above $1 million as a new tax because

Ban new taxes on personal property
Proposition 42 would make it much harder to create a wealth tax in California by prohibiting new taxes on the mere ownership of assets such as investment accounts, business interests and personal property — assets that are typically only taxed when they are sold or generate income. Like Proposition 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), which also attempts to block Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 42 would nullify Proposition 40 if it receives more votes, even if the billionaire tax also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

The measure’s ultra-wealthy backers say California should not tax people for merely owning or controlling retirement accounts, financial portfolios, or valuable personal possessions like art. They want to prevent taxes on unrealized gains — paper wealth that hasn’t been sold or generated taxable revenue — warning that pensions and retirement accounts could one day be taxed on their future value.
Oppose
The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, which is the sponsor of Prop. 40. The union argues that Prop. 42 is designed to trick voters into making it impossible to apply a wealth tax to billionaires. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on everyday people, the union says; instead, it’s a way for billionaires to avoid paying a one-time tax on their huge wealth.

the existing additional income tax is
temporary and will not continue post-2030 unless voters remove its sunset. Notably,
Proposition 42 does not specify how its exemption clause applies to extensions of this sort.
Taxpayers thus may be able to argue that Proposition 41 prohibits the tax imposed
by Proposition 3 because the latter is a tax “on the ownership or control” of property.
Because Proposition 42 never defines “ownership or control,” its protected category
potentially encompasses all income-producing personal property; it is a longstanding
income tax principle that income from a property is taxed “to the one who controls it.” For
example, consider the current treatment of stock options one earns as part of one’s job.
Such options are treated as labor income and, if exercised years later, a formula is used to
assess how much of their appreciation should be attributed to California.22 A court might
21 California broadly conforms to the positive tax benefits given to retirement savings by the federal
tax code. See generally Ca. Rev. and Tax Code 17501 et seq. Further, any reduction in these benefits
granted by California tax law would require a 2/3 supermajority. Cal. Constit. Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
Proposition 40 does not change any of this and, in fact, explicitly exempts true retirement assets.
See Proposition 40, Proposed Section 50303(c)(7).
22 See Cal. Code Regs. tit. 18, section 17951-5(b).
9
treat the post-2030 taxation of that option appreciation, or even of capital gains generally,
as a tax on the ownership or control of “financial assets” that is grandfathered only through
2030.
Proposition 42 could also arguably void Proposition 3 entirely if Proposition 42 gets
more votes. Proposition 42 has a sweeping conflicts provision (Sec. 5(a)) that could be read
to trigger if Proposition 3 were interpreted as permitting any form of taxation prohibited
by Proposition 42. Note further in regard to this that California adjudicators have recently
read formal tax terms, such as “unitary business,”23 “gross receipts,”24 and “agricultural
business activity,”25 in ways the drafters of those terms plainly did not anticipate, and
“personal property” could well follow a similar pattern.26
Moreover, Proposition 42 separately prohibits a post-2025 tax that “operates
retroactively to result in tax liability based on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred
or was present prior to the effective date” of the law. Sec. 2(a)(1). A court could hold that
this clause applies where post-2030 taxes fall on gains that accrued, or on equity
compensation earned, in earlier years. If so, the post-2030 rates could not be collected with
respect to income deemed attributable to earlier years, such as gain reflecting appreciation
that accrued before 2031 or compensation from services performed earlier. This could
substantially undermine the revenue-raising capacity of Prop 3. And a ruling of this kind
would also satisfy the second trigger of Proposition 42's conflicts provision, and so (as
discussed above), could result in all of Prop 3 being nullified.
Other Taxes
Proposition 42’s restrictions as to the taxation of other assets are very broad and
might impact a variety of current taxes or those that might reasonably be proposed. For
example, consider the bar on taxing “personal property.” This would, on its face, seem to
apply to the Vehicle License Fee, which is a tax on personal property.27 This fee is so
important to local governments that it was guaranteed to them by Prop 30 (Art. XIII, Sec.
36(b)(2)) and the allocation of its revenues to local governments is protected elsewhere in
23 Garcia-Rojas et al. v. Franchise Tax Board, A172054 (Cal. Ct. App. May 1, 2026).
24 Appeal of Microsoft Corp. and Subsidiaries, 2024-OTA-130 (Cal. Off. Tax App. July 27, 2023).
25 Smithfield Packaged Meats Corp. v. California Franchise Tax Board, No. 21STCV39637 (Cal. Super.
Ct. 2026) (final statement of decision).
26 We do not mean to imply here that we agree with these decisions, but the fact remains that a
certain rigid formalism seems appealing to the California judiciary sometimes.
27 Now, there is some complexity here because the VLF was held in 1936 not to be a tax on personal
property but a tax on a privilege. See Ingels v. Riley, 5 Cal. 2d. 154 (1936). But Prop 42 would seem
to apply to a privilege tax.
10
the constitution, which requires the state to backfill localities if the rate falls below 0.65%
(Art. XI, Sec. 15). Given that the current rate of the VLF (0.65%) is lower than the rate that
it was long before, and the sound policy reasons why the rate should at least be the same as
the rate for real property (1%), Prop 42 will interfere with the Legislature or the people
increasing this tax. While Prop 13 doesn’t leave much room for maneuver on real estate
taxes, Proposition 42 would constrict that freedom even further by apparently prohibiting
any future state changes, absent a constitutional amendment.
Retroactivity
Prop 42’s limit on retroactive taxes will also make future tax reform harder and less
effective. Again, the only real policy payoff of this provision is to sink the billionaire tax; the
Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment of the federal constitution already bars states
from engaging in unreasonable retroactive taxation.28 In many cases good tax policy
requires that new taxes apply to at least some transactions that happened before the tax
was adopted. New taxes are often effective prior to enactment date in order to prevent
arbitrage or other evasive transactions before the tax can go into effect. Other retroactive
measures may simply fix a mistake or close off an unintended tax shelter that taxpayers
have been exploiting, as in the leading Supreme Court cases. In other cases, going back to
sometime before enactment of the tax may ensure a more accurate measure of the tax base.
For example, the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did just that.29 Having a tax change be
retroactive to the start of the year is also a way to start raising revenue immediately should
that be desired. All of these practices are longstanding and common and flow from the
states’ inherent power to control their own revenue systems.
Prop 42’s retroactivity bar could also further complicate health care financing
legislation. Provider fee statutes are sometimes written so that they apply to periods that
begin before enactment, with collection following once federal approval arrives. A post-
2025 statute with this structure could thus be threatened by Prop 42, Sec. 2(a)(1). The
existing hospital fee framework predates 2026 and thus has a grandfather defense
shielding it from these threats,30 but this defense does not protect future bills that may
reach backward, and so drafters will face new constraints and risks if Prop 42 passes.
Conclusion
California’s public finance rules are already exceptionally baroque. This irrational
opacity is particularly harmful considering that California’s underlying tax bases have not
28 United States v. Carlton, 512 U.S. 26 (1994).
29 26 USC 965(a)(1).
30 Sec. 2(b).
11
been substantially reformed for a century and the state has many urgent needs. Both
Propositions 41 and 42 add even more complexity to this rickety system, which, by itself,
should be avoided. As it is, the complicated and vague new rules that would be imposed by
Propositions 41 and 42 are likely to make it much harder to finance all manner of public
goods going forward.

# Endorsement: Reject Prop. 4. Don’t let politicians raid public funds for their campaigns.
## Taxpayer dollars must stay reserved to fix municipal roads and parks, rather than finance elections
...
The influence of money on political races has gotten out of control, but allowing candidates to accept public funds — taxpayer dollars — for campaign purposes is not the answer.
We recommend voting “no” on Proposition 4.
Our tax dollars should not be spent on election campaigns.
## Related Articles
#### Sky-high spending
Consider this news organization’s report last week showing how a single political action committee backed by billionaires — Building a Better California — has spent nearly a quarter of a billion dollars this year alone, breaking all previous records.
Understandably alarmed, this inundation of money into state politics has pushed legislators to ask voters this November to repeal a 1988 law and allow taxpayer dollars to be spent on campaigns.
A “yes” vote would allow state and local governments to create programs so that public funds — again, taxpayer dollars — could be set aside for election campaigns.
We understand the desire to take corporate money out of elections.

Here are our recommendations, so far, for the most competitive races and significant ballot measures on Bay Area voters’ Nov. 3 ballots. To reach our conclusions, we have interviewed more than 70 candidates for federal, state, county, city and school district offices as well as the leaders of committees supporting and opposing initiatives. Please know that, per company policy, we do not endorse in gubernatorial races; and given editorial resources, we prioritize making endorsements in open-seat, or non-incumbent, races. Bookmark this page to view additional endorsements as they are published between now and election day.
Statewide offices
Lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/10/endorsement-elect-fiona-ma-states-next-lieutenant-governor/)
Success as this state’s No. 2 requires understanding its levers of power. Currently treasurer, Fiona Ma already knows how to leverage them. The next lieutenant governor must be as capable of navigating uncharted waters as the governor whom she or he might need to replace at a moment’s notice. By that standard, Fiona Ma is eminently qualified.
(Our interviews with the two candidates for lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma and Gloria Romero — are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/25/in-their-words-fiona-ma-v-gloria-romero-we-asked-they-answered/).)
Treasurer — Eleni Kounalakis (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/endorsement-elect-eleni-kounalakis-californias-next-treasurer/)
California’s next treasurer should expect to inherit the most financially volatile environment since the Great Recession. The state faces long-running structural shortfalls. Growing federal deficits will likely drive up the state’s borrowing costs. Counties are scrambling to fill gaps in once-federally funded services. Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis’ record in business, politics and diplomacy is public and extensive. There are few blanks to fill in. The challenges awaiting the next treasurer require a tested policy and economic operator. That is Lt. Gov. Kounalakis.
(Our interview with Eleni Kounalakis is here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/in-their-words-kounalakis-caballero-tell-us-why-they-can-manage-californias-162-billion/). Jennifer Hawks would not complete our interview request or provide her resume after repeated requests.)
Insurance commissioner — Ben Allen (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/endorsement-elect-ben-allen-californias-next-insurance-commissioner/)
Bay Area voters must understand: When they choose termed-out Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara’s successor, the viability of homeownership is what’s really on the ballot. The conditions for deadlier and most destructive wildfires keep growing. And there is no end in sight. There is only one candidate who grasps the complexity of this crisis and has the legislative experience to address it. That is Ben Allen.
(Our interviews with insurance commissioner candidates Ben Allen and Jane Kim are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/in-their-words-these-candidates-want-to-control-your-home-insurance-heres-why-and-what-theyll-do/).)
Superintendent of Public Instruction — Richard Barrera (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-elect-richard-barrera-californias-superintendent-of-public-instruction-november-election-california-public-schools-sonja-shaw/)
California schools face a constellation of challenges, including declining enrollment, shrinking budgets and persistent achievement gaps. Richard Barrera is a detail-oriented incrementalist focused on student absenteeism and mental health. His opponent, Sonja Shaw, is a brash culture warrior more interested in girls’ locker rooms than the nitty gritty of school reform. We support Barrera.
(Our interviews with Richard Barrera and Sonja Shaw are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/richard-barrera-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/) and here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/sonja-shaw-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/), respectively.)
California ballot measures
Prop. 1 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/)
This initiative puts state taxpayers in debt for 25 years and pumps money into a bloated system. Under the best of circumstances, it would add a tiny fraction of the new housing supply needed all while doing next to nothing to solve the real problem: the inexcusably exorbitant cost of building affordable housing.
Prop. 2 — Yes
California’s budget rules perversely count saving as spending, limiting state Legislators’ capacities to bank windfalls for leaner years. That’s fiscal malpractice written into the Constitution. Proposition 2 would exempt rainy day fund deposits from the Gann Limit, double the fund’s cap and require larger deposits when capital gains revenues surge. A state with volatile tax revenues needs a bigger cushion, not obstacles to saving.
Prop. 3 — Yes (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/endorsement-proposition-3-california-ballot-measure-progressive-income-tax/)
California’s richest are doing great. Over the last four decades, while the bottom four-fifths of households have seen their real incomes decline, the top 1% have seen their real incomes grow two and half times. This upper stratum now earns in a week what the middle fifth of Californians make in a year. Proposition 3 asks the Californians truly living the California dream — the highest 2% of earners — to keep paying their fair share while also helping the state avoid painful cuts to services induced by President Trump’s and House Republicans’ deliberately punitive H.R. 1, or the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Prop. 4 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/19/endorsement-reject-prop-4-dont-let-politicians-raid-public-funds-for-their-campaigns/)
Taxpayer dollars must stay reserved to fix municipal roads and parks, rather than finance elections.
Prop. 5 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/20/endorsement-no-on-prop-5-a-bad-idea-that-protects-the-status-quo-and-silences-independent-minded-challengers/)
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Prop. 37 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/)
This measure looks great on the surface. But all that glitters isn’t gold. It would give builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it would artificially inflate the market by putting borrowed cash into buyers’ hands. Instead of lowering construction costs, this merely helps California home buyers take on more debt in the form of second mortgages.
Prop. 38 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/endorsement-no-on-california-proposition-38-an-8-4-billion-money-grab-immunotherapy-ucla-research-ballot-measure/)
This deceptive ballot measure is an $8.4 billion money grab that would funnel taxpayer funds to a single private medical institute run by a billionaire, who is also the chief backer of the Proposition 38 campaign.
Prop. 39 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/15/endorsement-reject-proposition-39-voter-id-fraud-ballot-measure/)
Our editorial board repeatedly asked the Yes on Proposition 39 campaign for evidence of voter fraud in California, rampant or otherwise, and they deflected, dodged and denied the premise of our questions. In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots (among other restrictive voting rules and audits), it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding and repeatedly debunked claims that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. is an expensive solution to a phantom problem. Reject Proposition 39.
Prop. 40 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/21/endorsement-reject-california-ballot-propositions-40-41-42-billionaires-tax-ai-inequality/)
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts. However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem. We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging measure — the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Prop. 41 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/21/endorsement-reject-california-ballot-propositions-40-41-42-billionaires-tax-ai-inequality/)
The problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago. California has changed radically since the 1970s. And its fiscal rules must leave the state with the flexibility to address issues voters of the era never had to deal with — six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs. The state must not surrender its future freedom of action to defeat a single, one-time tax proposal.
Prop. 42 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/21/endorsement-reject-california-ballot-propositions-40-41-42-billionaires-tax-ai-inequality/)
Proposition 42 was written by this tech boom’s beneficiaries, who are now among the wealthiest humans in history. If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. However, amid this era’s technology- and climate-induced uncertainty, California must keep its options open. This measure would needlessly and recklessly narrow them.
Prop. 43 — Yes (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/17/endorsement-back-prop-43-restore-voter-approved-restrictions-on-local-taxes-proposition-13/)
California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them. Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
Prop. 44 — No (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-prop-44-politics-dont-belong-in-californias-community-health-clinics-november-3-general-election-california-health-care/)
Proposition 44 would require California’s 2,000 safety net clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient care and the services that support it, and to report publicly how their money is spent. On the surface, that sounds great. However, if passed, the measure would push the majority of clinics across California into the red — many of which have spent the last six years clawing their way back from the brink of the pandemic.
Prop. 45 —Yes (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/16/endorsement-proposition-45-november3-ballot-initiative-ceqa-reform-housing-costs/)
Proposition 45 won’t transform the state’s regulatory maze overnight. But it would make California’s planning approval process fairer, less expensive and considerably more predictable.
Bay Area transit tax
Measure RTM — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/)
Bay Area voters, threatened with a transportation apocalypse if they don’t approve a billion-dollar-a-year sales tax increase for public transit, should just say no. Measure RTM on the Nov. 3 ballot would add 0.5% to the cost of goods for the next 14 years in Alameda, Contra Costa, Santa Clara and San Mateo counties and 1% in San Francisco. Opposing the initiative is not a vote against public transit. It’s a demand for responsible financial management.
U.S. Congress
Congressional District 14 — Aisha Wahab (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/07/endorsement-elect-aisha-wahab-to-replace-ex-rep-eric-swalwell-in-congress/)
Among the two candidates left vying for ex-Rep. Eric Swalwell’s seat, Rep. Aisha Wahab is the best choice to represent Alameda County. The U.S. Congress is no place to send a novice. Former state Senator Wahab isn’t one. As the assistant majority leader, she was the third most powerful lawmaker in the California Senate. In that chamber, the 39-year-old Democrat had a front-row seat to the affordability debates affecting this district, which includes Hayward, Fremont, Castro Valley and Livermore. There is only one reliable, proven candidate in this race. That’s Wahab. (Wahab has represented the East Bay in Congress since September after defeating Melissa Hernandez in an August runoff to temporarily occupy Swalwell’s vacant seat. The Nov. 3 election will determine who will permanently represent the district.)
(Our interviews with candidates running to replace ex-Rep. Eric Swalwell — Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez — are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/07/candidates-14th-district-alameda-county-swalwell-seat/).)
California Legislature
State Senate District 10 — Scott Sakakihara
The Union City councilmember is a thoughtful policy wonk who provided our editorial board with detailed answers to the district’s biggest challenges: housing costs, homelessness, struggling schools, fragmented transit systems, etc. Sakakihara — a Harvard-educated US Navy Reserve officer, Democrat and former Palantir executive — explained how he would speed housing approvals, strengthen student mental health services and demand results for taxpayers’ money. His Republican opponent, Linda Price, remains a relative unknown. Price refused multiple requests to provide her resume or answer our questionnaire. Send Sakakihara to represent this diverse, million-person district, which includes Hayward, Newark and Fremont in the north and Santa Clara, Sunnyvale and San Jose in the south.
(Our interview with Scott Sakakihara is here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/26/scott-sakakihara-state-senatorial-candidate-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/).)
San Jose City Council
District 5 — Peter Ortiz (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-peter-ortiz-bien-doan-and-genny-altwer-to-san-jose-city-council/)
Over the last four years, Councilmember Peter Ortiz has evolved from an activist into a governance-focused lawmaker and forceful defender of the city’s immigrants.
District 7 — Bien Doan (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-peter-ortiz-bien-doan-and-genny-altwer-to-san-jose-city-council/)
Councilmember Bien Doan, a retired firefighter first elected four years ago, is ideologically idiosyncratic. Doan identifies as pro-business but he has led fights against wage theft. He’s pro-single-family housing but has defended tenant protections for mobile home residents. He told our editorial board that in his next term he would prioritize increasing police staffing and cutting business red tape. Doan’s rival — East Side Union High School District Trustee Van Le — is not a serious candidate. This is her third time running for this seat, and her main policy platform appears to be opposing Doan.
District 9 — Genny Altwer (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/endorsement-san-jose-needs-a-blight-fighter-elect-genny-altwer-to-city-council/)
This district in the southwest corner of San Jose – which includes Cambrian Park, Hillsdale, Kirk Park and parts of Willow Glen – does not have the same degree of vacant storefronts, job losses, blight and homelessness as other parts of this city. But it is not immune. Whoever replaces Vice Mayor Pam Foley must be able to address this 100,000-person district’s concerns while helping solve citywide problems. We believe that candidate is Genny Altwer. Altwer, 45, represents neither the status quo nor a radical break from it. Her unconventional resume should bring new thinking to old policies.
(Our interviews with candidates Genny Altwer and Gordon Chester are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/26/gordon-chester-candidate-for-san-jose-city-council-district-9-answers-the-mercury-news-primary-questionnaire/).)
San Jose Unified School District
Area 4 — Michael Melillo (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-michael-melillo-to-san-jose-unified-school-district-board-of-education/)
Brian Wheatley is retiring after eight years on the San Jose Unified School District Board of Education, leaving his seat up for grabs on Nov. 3. Two candidates are running to fill his place representing Area 4 in the city’s southwest: Michael Melillo, a former trustee and Apple data scientist, and Mary Grunthaner, a retired history teacher. Between the two, Melillo, whose two children attend schools in the district, is best equipped to tackle the district’s financial challenges with analytical thoroughness. Instead of making haphazard cuts, Melillo’s data-driven strategy would safeguard schools performing in the top quadrant of the California state dashboard with active PTAs and high numbers of English learners and foster youth.
Santa Clara
Jed York’s San Francisco 49ers — has spent millions trying to turn this South Bay suburb into its subsidiary. Unfortunately, a majority of Santa Clara’s seven-member City Council has all too willingly obliged. Santa Clara needs a clean break. It needs independent voices who will stand up to this $11 billion football franchise and move beyond its crippling past grievances. On Nov. 3, voters should elect David Kertes for mayor, Yvonne Inciarte for City Council District 2 and Eric Crutchlow for District 3.
Mayor — David Kertes (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/31/endorsement-break-the-49ers-grip-over-santa-clara-make-kertes-mayor-elect-inciarte-and-crutchlow-to-council/)
District 2 — Yvonne Inciarte (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/31/endorsement-break-the-49ers-grip-over-santa-clara-make-kertes-mayor-elect-inciarte-and-crutchlow-to-council/)

I now have a comprehensive picture. Let me summarize my analysis and reach a decision.

**Prop 42 (Nov 2026): "Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026"**

What it does:
1. Adds new Article VIII to the California Constitution banning any state law or constitutional provision enacted on/after Jan 1, 2026 from imposing a tax "on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" — defined to include pensions, 401(k)s, IRAs, mutual funds, and ALL personal property, tangible or intangible: financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property, personal belongings.
2. Bans retroactive taxes (with narrow exceptions only for legislative statutes, ≤365 days, tied to a governor-declared emergency). No exception for voter initiatives.
3. Conflict clause: if Prop 42 outpolls Prop 40, Prop 40 is "null and void" in its entirety.
4. Legal defense provision (independent counsel, continuous General Fund appropriation).

Funding: ~$157M to the Yes committee, ~99% from Building a Better California, whose top donors are Sergey Brin ($102M+) and other billionaires (Doerr, Schmidt, Collison) who would personally owe billions under Prop 40. LA Times: the four richest Californians (Brin, Huang, Page, Zuckerberg) would owe ~40% of the estimated $107B. Brin's own spending is <1% of his estimated tax bill.

Oppose: ~$32-34M, nearly all SEIU-UHW.

Key evaluation:

**Against (NO):**
1. **Manufactured premise.** Prop 40 explicitly exempts pensions and retirement accounts (Prop 40 §50303(c)(7); LAO confirms: "Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded"). California does not currently tax ownership of financial assets, and there is no serious pending proposal to tax ordinary people's 401(k)s. The "protect your retirement" framing is a decoy — acknowledged even by conservative-leaning analysts.
2. **Grossly overbroad relative to its stated purpose.** It doesn't just protect retirement accounts; it constitutionally bans ANY future state tax on ownership/control of any personal property — business interests, intellectual property, digital assets, personal belongings. That is a permanent removal of an entire tax category from the state's toolkit, reversible only by another statewide vote.
3. **Self-dealing, anti-democratic mechanism.** Its decisive provision is a poison pill that lets a measure outpolling Prop 40 by even one vote void a majority-approved tax in its entirety. If you oppose the billionaire tax, you can simply vote NO on Prop 40 — no constitutional entrenchment needed. Prop 42's marginal function is purely to override a majority.
